clinicalPearls: A rare vegetating variant of pemphigus vulgaris characterised by hypertrophic, verrucous, exudative plaques favouring intertriginous and periorificial sites.
Two forms are described: the Neumann type, which begins with flaccid bullae and erosions that evolve into vegetations, and the milder Hallopeau type, which starts with pustules.
Flexural predilection includes the axillae, groin, inframammary folds, perianal region and the angles of the mouth; the scalp and face may also be affected.
Oral mucosal involvement is common and may include cerebriform changes of the tongue, mirroring the mucosal disease of pemphigus vulgaris.
Histology shows suprabasal acantholysis with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and characteristic intraepidermal eosinophilic microabscesses.
Direct immunofluorescence demonstrates intercellular IgG and C3 in a net-like (chicken-wire) pattern, and serum antibodies target desmoglein 3 (and often desmoglein 1).
The Hallopeau type generally follows a more indolent course and may respond to lower doses of systemic therapy than classical pemphigus vulgaris.
Systemic corticosteroids with steroid-sparing immunosuppressants remain the mainstay, with rituximab increasingly used for refractory or steroid-dependent disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Pemphigus vegetans is a clinical and histological variant of pemphigus vulgaris driven by IgG autoantibodies against the desmosomal cadherins desmoglein 3 and, in many cases, desmoglein 1. Antibody binding disrupts desmosomal adhesion between keratinocytes, producing suprabasal acantholysis and flaccid blistering. At intertriginous and periorificial sites, the warm moist environment and chronic irritation are thought to provoke an exuberant reparative epidermal response, giving rise to pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and the characteristic vegetating plaques studded with eosinophilic microabscesses. The reason certain patients develop vegetating rather than classical lesions is incompletely understood but may reflect host reactive patterns and local factors.
additionalDifferentials: granular parakeratosis and intertrigo with candidiasis
additionalInvestigations: lesional biopsy for histopathology (suprabasal acantholysis, eosinophilic microabscesses, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia)
perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence (intercellular IgG and C3)
indirect immunofluorescence for circulating intercellular antibodies
ELISA for desmoglein 1 and desmoglein 3 antibodies
swabs and culture to exclude secondary bacterial or candidal infection
syphilis serology when perianal or genital vegetations raise suspicion of condylomata lata
baseline screening prior to immunosuppression (glucose, blood pressure, infection screen)
redFlags: extensive erosions with fluid loss, secondary infection or sepsis
severe oropharyngeal involvement limiting oral intake and nutrition
rapid progression or transformation to widespread classical pemphigus vulgaris
signs of systemic infection arising from immunosuppressive therapy
reference.prognosis: With appropriate immunosuppression the disease is controllable, and the Hallopeau type in particular may follow a relatively benign, indolent course; however relapses are frequent and the Neumann type can be chronic and difficult to clear.
pitfalls: Mistaking flexural vegetations for intertrigo, candidiasis or condylomata lata and delaying biopsy.
Biopsying only the vegetating surface and missing diagnostic acantholysis at the edge.
Overlooking oral disease that may be the earliest and most persistent manifestation.
Attributing treatment failure to disease when secondary bacterial or candidal colonisation is driving the plaques.
Assuming the milder Hallopeau course applies to all patients and under-treating Neumann-type disease.
